newsitem.title: JAPAN: Bundesbank against softening EMU terms -- Schieber.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank against softening EMU terms -- Schieber.

text.p: Helmut Schieber, a member of the Bundesbank Directorate, said on Thursday that the German central bank was "explicitly" against softening criteria for admission to the Economic economic and monetary union (EMU).
He was speaking at an EMU seminar in Tokyo.

"All political institutions, including parliament, government, political parties, constitutional courts and of course, the Bundesbank, are explicitly against this solution (and softening convergence criteria)," he said.
He added that this feeling was shared by other potential EMU member nations.
"Less than two months ago, the European Council stressed that the criteria of sustainable convergence and the requirement of central bank independence must be strictly applied," he said.
Schieber also said that "from a technical point of view, EMU is within the envisaged timetable apart from a few details".

He noted that a month ago conceptual work was concluded for the main issues of relevance to the conduct of single monetary policy and a so-called framework report was published by the European Monetary Institute (EMI).
He said that there are two main reasons why softening of the criteria would not be acceptable or practicable.

"The financial markets are watching the convergence process with keen interest and they have responded time and again to political and economic doubts about the convergence process, with, in some cases, violent attacks on exchange rates," Schieber said.

"In the case of any feared or imminent softening of the strict convergence concept, a new and possibly even more severe crisis might threaten, which in the end might jeopardise the entire project," he said.

He also said that countries with relatively low long-term interest rates such as Germany, the Netherlands and Austria would find it difficult to accept the inclusion of some countries which may not meet the convergence criteria and which often have higher long-term interest rates.

He said that if they are included in the first round, this might result in higher rates in low interest rate countries. This could lead to problems such as capital flight to other countries, which could lead to exchange-rate problems.
He said that he is confident the euro can compete with the dollar and the yen but only if the technical preparation work has been done.
